title: the being at the gate
hookLine: a gigantic being blocks the gate of the sleeping camp, and every weapon Ashvatthama throws disappears into it
carry: Shiva ends what has had its time
tomorrow: the night the Pandavas were away

cards: The Pandava camp is dark and quiet. Ashvatthama reaches the gate with Kripa and Kritavarma behind him. And the gate isn't empty.

Something is standing there, so large it seems to fill the night. In Ganguli's English it's a being of enormous size, terrible to look at, blazing, wrapped in a tiger skin, with snakes for ornaments and many eyes.
It doesn't speak. It just stands between Ashvatthama and the sleeping camp.

teach.b: Ashvatthama does what a warrior does. He attacks. He hurls weapon after weapon at the being, and it swallows them all and stands untouched.

Empty-handed, he thinks of the advice he ignored, in effect: whoever turns from the counsel of friends who wish him well comes to grief. Then he turns to Mahadeva, the great god, Shiva, and praises him with many names.
A golden altar appears with a fire blazing on it, and Shiva's fierce companions crowd around.
Ashvatthama offers the only thing he has left, himself, and steps into the fire.

Shiva appears and speaks plainly: he has protected the Panchalas until now, out of regard for Krishna, but their time is over. He gives Ashvatthama a sword and enters into him. Here's why this matters for Hindus.
Shiva is the god who brings things to an end. Many Hindus speak of God's three great works: Brahma creates, Vishnu sustains, Shiva dissolves. That last work isn't evil.

It clears the ground for what comes next, which is why Shiva is also called Mahakala, great Time, and why he is honored at the cremation ground, where a life is given back. In this book, Shiva says a time has ended.
But the epic doesn't let Ashvatthama hide behind that: in two days, Krishna will hold him answerable. So a Hindu can say two things at once. Endings belong to God.
What we do in them still belongs to us.

how: Hindus who worship Shiva as Mahadeva call on him by many names, and the hymn Ashvatthama offers at the gate is one of the places in the Mahabharata where those names are gathered.

o: the golden altar where Ashvatthama offers his hymn
the night book, where a being at the gate swallows weapons
the great god's name, called on at the camp's gate

games.q: at the gate — tap the pairs.
p: said the Panchalas' time was over

s: Hindus see Shiva's work of dissolving as evil
it is one of God's three great works, clearing room for what comes next.
Ashvatthama offered himself into the fire
with nothing left, he stepped into the fire on the golden altar.
Shiva said he had never protected the Panchalas
he said he had protected them out of regard for Krishna, but their time was over.

games.q: a friend hears this story and asks why anyone would pray to Shiva, a god of destruction. what's the Hindu answer?
o: Shiva is the dark side; you pray so he leaves you alone.
Shiva dissolves what has had its time, so something new can come.
Shiva only matters in this one story.
games.why: Brahma creates, Vishnu sustains, Shiva dissolves: endings belong to God too. and Ashvatthama still answers for what he does.

practice: Om namah shivaya is one of the most loved prayers in Hinduism: a bow to Shiva. Sit tall and bring to mind something in your life that is ending, or has ended.
Breathing slowly, say the prayer silently, once on each out-breath, and let the ending be held by something larger than you. If you don't pray, breathe out slowly and simply let the ending be named.

wordCard.voice: Sauptika. The night book, where a being guards the gate, and Shiva, lord of endings, says a time is over.

orig.note: Mahadeva, 'the great god': a name for Shiva, the god Ashvatthama turns to at the gate.

carryVoice: Your line: Shiva ends what has had its time. Tomorrow, the night itself. Day eight hundred fifty-two, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva, the being at the gate, Ashvatthama's weapons swallowed, his reflection on ignored counsel, his hymn to Mahadeva, the golden altar, his self-offering and Shiva entering him
